claims.claim: Martin says he has always written in tight third person because that is how people perceive: we see events from our own eyes and hear only our own thoughts.

claims.quote: I've always written from a tight third-person point of view

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a strong believer in a limited but very tight third person and says he hates the omniscient viewpoint because no one has one.
claims.source: Adria's News interview (2012-10-08), repost
claims.quote: limited but very tight third person point of view

claims.claim: Each POV chapter is written in a different voice and style; Martin says he switches voice every time he switches chapters.
claims.source: Entertainment Weekly (James Hibberd, 2018-11-19) via Winter Is Coming
claims.quote: I switch voices every time I switch chapters.

claims.claim: Moving from Tyrion chapters to Jon Snow chapters is a whole different voice, and Martin struggles for days to recover a character's voice after switching.
claims.source: Austin Chronicle, Amy Gentry interview (2013-08-29)
claims.quote: it's a whole different voice

claims.claim: Martin does not write chapters in reading order; because shifting voices is hard he drafts two to four consecutive chapters of the same character.
claims.source: Adria's News interview (2012-10-08), repost
claims.quote: write consecutively two, three or four chapters

claims.claim: Martin says multiple viewpoints are essential so the reader sees a conflict from both sides' self-justifications rather than a cartoon Dark Lord.
claims.source: Locus Online interview excerpts (Nov 2005)
claims.quote: Having multiple viewpoints is crucial to the grayness of the characters.

claims.claim: Apparent contradictions between chapters are deliberate: two characters remember an event differently because of the point-of-view structure and the unreliable narrator.
claims.source: The Atlantic, Rachael Brown interview (July 2011)
claims.quote: the point of view structure and the unreliable narrator

claims.claim: Martin describes his method as seeing everything only through the eyes of the viewpoint characters, a discipline he links to structure learned in television.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: seeing everything through the eyes only of the viewpoint characters

claims.feature: first viewpoint character as decoy hero
claims.claim: Martin opens with Bran as the first viewpoint so readers assume he is the young-Arthur hero, then defenestrates him to signal this is not the familiar story.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: Bran is the first viewpoint character.

claims.claim: For battles Martin alternates between dropping the reader into the carnage from a private's viewpoint and looking down from a general's vantage.
claims.source: Interview with George R. R. Martin, bernardcornwell.net (undated)
claims.quote: Sometimes I employ the private's viewpoint

claims.claim: Martin traces the interwoven multi-POV structure of the novels to the Wild Cards mosaic novels, likening it to a Robert Altman film in prose.
claims.source: nekoplz.com interview (Jay, undated)
claims.quote: Robert Altman film in prose

claims.claim: Martin modeled the general construction on The Lord of the Rings: begin small, accumulate characters, then send them on separate paths.
claims.source: The Atlantic, Rachael Brown interview (July 2011)
claims.quote: Tolkien begins very small, in the Shire

claims.feature: register: modern prose with a pinch of archaism
claims.claim: Martin says the line between modern prose and archaic diction is fine; his compromise is modern prose stripped of pop-culture references with occasional archaic words, like salt in soup.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: modern prose, but omitting all pop culture references

claims.claim: After his editor feared a 'forsooth' would follow, Martin kept 'mayhaps' for old characters like Aemon and gave younger ones like Bran 'perhaps' and 'maybe'.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: a "forsooth" would follow shortly

claims.feature: period register by reading period syntax
claims.claim: For Fevre Dream Martin read period novels such as Twain's to absorb their syntax and vocabulary, a different register strategy from the one used in Ice and Fire.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: to understand the syntax and words

claims.claim: Unlike Tolkien, Martin invents only the words he needs (he says about eight Dothraki words) and admits he fakes the rest.
claims.source: IGN interview (May 2019) via Winter Is Coming (2019-05-14)
claims.quote: He invented entire languages, I just fake it.

claims.feature: names as slant-variants with phonetic power
claims.claim: Martin makes names up as variants of real ones (Eddard for Edward) and insists on the right sound, holding that a name evokes a character better than a page of description.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Naming Characters correspondence (2003-04-01)
claims.quote: variants of real names -- Eddard for Edward

claims.feature: names: Vance and Tolkien as models
claims.claim: Asked about names, Martin points the fan to Jack Vance and Tolkien as the masters of evocative naming.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Naming Characters correspondence (2003-04-01)
claims.quote: He's marvelous with names.

claims.claim: Martin denies that Ice and Fire is Vancean; he tried once to write like Vance and concluded only Vance can, keeping his own plainer voice.
claims.source: Infinity Plus, Nick Gevers interview (Feb 2001)
claims.quote: Vance has his voice and I have mine.

claims.feature: Vance admired for ear for language
claims.claim: What Martin says sets Vance apart is style, imagination, world building and an ear for names and language.
claims.source: nekoplz.com interview (Jay, undated)
claims.quote: His ear for names, for language.

claims.claim: Martin says his early style piled on adjectives, mistaking verbosity for richness, until journalism-school professors struck them out.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: if one adjective was good, three were better

claims.claim: Hearing actors read his long speeches taught Martin to write shorter back-and-forth dialogue instead of page-long monologues.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: much shorter back and forth kind of dialogue

claims.claim: Martin credits his television years with sharpening his dialogue.
claims.source: January Magazine profile, Linda L. Richards (Jan 2001)
claims.quote: I think working in Hollywood sharpened my dialog.

claims.claim: Martin says screenwriting is easier than prose because, per William Goldman, it is all structure and dialogue, and that working in TV improved both in his novels.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: It's all structure, structure and dialogue.

claims.claim: Martin carries television act breaks into chapter endings: each should close on a cliffhanger, a twist point, or a new revelation.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: just a twist point or a new revelation

claims.claim: Though no volume resolves the whole, Martin tries to give each book a sense of completion like a symphony movement wrapping up.
claims.source: Locus Online interview excerpts (Nov 2005)
claims.quote: a movement of the symphony has wrapped up

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a very visual writer who sees a scene in his head the way a director sees a shot.
claims.source: January Magazine profile, Linda L. Richards (Jan 2001)
claims.quote: much as a director would see a shot

claims.feature: chapter opening from a seed sentence
claims.claim: The first chapter came to Martin whole; its first sentence's phrase 'summer snows' told him seasons were wrong here, and the world grew outward from that sentence.
claims.source: CBS 60 Minutes, Anderson Cooper (2019-04-14)
claims.quote: They find the direwolf pups in the summer snows.

claims.claim: Martin does not build the world first; the map took half an hour and the world-building grew parallel to the writing.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: I don't build the world first, then write in it.

claims.claim: Martin defends feasts, clothes and heraldry as necessary because a novel is an immersive experience; detail and showing-not-telling are required and nothing is gratuitous.
claims.source: The Atlantic, Rachael Brown interview (July 2011)
claims.quote: detail is necessary, showing not telling is necessary

claims.claim: Martin says if his sex is gratuitous then so are his violence, feasting, clothes and heraldry, since little of it advances plot and plot is not why one reads novels.
claims.source: The Atlantic, Rachael Brown interview (July 2011)
claims.quote: gratuitous feasting, and gratuitous description of clothes

claims.claim: In the cookbook foreword Martin says he wants readers to live with the story rather than read it, and to taste the food when they sit at his table.
claims.source: Official Game of Thrones Cookbook foreword via ComicBook.com (Nicole Drum, 2024-05-04)
claims.quote: I want them to taste the food.

claims.claim: Martin frames fiction as emotion and vicarious experience, which is why sensory detail matters more than what characters are saying.
claims.source: Official Game of Thrones Cookbook foreword via ComicBook.com (Nicole Drum, 2024-05-04)
claims.quote: Fiction is about emotion. The heart, not the head.

claims.claim: Martin admits he enjoys heraldry for its own sake and plays fast and loose with real heraldic conventions.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Outland (Ottakars) interview (Sept 2000)
claims.quote: I enjoy the heraldry just for its own sake

claims.source: Infinity Plus, Nick Gevers interview (Feb 2001)
claims.quote: Besides, I like the heraldry.

claims.claim: Martin rejects both a Disney Middle Ages and thousands of pages of mud and lice; the real period had room for plagues and pageantry and he wants both, heightened.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Outland (Ottakars) interview (Sept 2000)
claims.quote: room for both plagues and pageantry

claims.claim: Martin describes the Middle Ages as chivalry beside brutality, castles over hovels, and tournament color rising out of a world of dung, dirt and plague.

claims.quote: a brown and grey world of dung, dirt, and plague

claims.feature: black-clad good guys to undermine convention

claims.source: So Spake Martin, Outland (Ottakars) interview (Sept 2000)
claims.quote: to undermine that annoying convention

claims.feature: historical-fiction grit fused with fantasy wonder
claims.claim: Martin says he wanted to combine the wonder and imagery of Tolkien fantasy with the gloom of historical fiction.
claims.source: Tolkien Society report of Edinburgh International Book Festival talk (2014-08-12)
claims.quote: the wonder and image of Tolkien fantasy

claims.claim: Martin faults Tolkien's imitators for taking medieval castles and princesses but writing them from a 20th-century point of view.
claims.source: Tolkien Society report of Edinburgh International Book Festival talk (2014-08-12)
claims.quote: writing it from a 20th-century point of view

claims.claim: On his own blog Martin restates the series' aim as blending epic fantasy's wonder with the grittiness of the best historical fiction, with much less magic than most fantasy.
claims.source: Not a Blog, 'Here There Be Dragons' (2024-07-11)
claims.quote: blend the wonder of epic fantasy with the grittiness

claims.claim: Martin describes historical fiction as grittier, harder-edged and more realistic than epic fantasy and says he set out to meld the two traditions.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: grittier, harder-edged, more realistic

claims.claim: Because history locks a writer in, Martin mixes sources and amplifies them, holding that fantasy must be bigger and brighter than life (Hadrian's Wall becomes seven hundred feet of ice).
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: fantasy always has to be a little bigger and brighter

claims.claim: Martin tells writers to think through every departure from real life (flying pigs change the pork industry) and to get armor, armies and horses right or readers will write.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: it's gonna change the pork industry

claims.claim: Martin contrasts Dunsany's once-upon-a-time mode with Tolkien's dynastic history and places his own work with Tolkien, closer to historical fiction.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: who was the king before him?

claims.claim: Martin says fantasy must be rooted in reality first, then played with and given its imaginative element.
claims.source: Bullseye / Sound of Young America, John Hodgman (2011-09-19)
claims.quote: In fantasy, you have to root it in reality.

claims.feature: fantasy prose as the language of dreams
claims.claim: Martin's credo essay holds that the best fantasy is written in the language of dreams and restores strong colors and spices that realism drains away.
claims.source: 'On Fantasy', georgerrmartin.com (1996)
claims.quote: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.

claims.claim: The essay opposes fantasy's rich colors and spices to the drab strip-mall real, implying a prose that reaches for vivid sensory nouns.
claims.source: 'On Fantasy', georgerrmartin.com (1996)
claims.quote: silver and scarlet, indigo and azure

claims.claim: Martin intentionally repeats phrases such as 'A Lannister always pays his debts' and remembered lines, a technique he says he took from Stephen King.
claims.source: Adria's News interview (2012-10-08), repost
claims.quote: I have learned this technique from Stephen King

claims.claim: Martin handles magic like salt in a stew, a little improving it and too much ruining it; elsewhere he says explicit magic ceases to be magical.
claims.source: Austin Chronicle, Amy Gentry interview (2013-08-29)
claims.quote: like a little salt in a stew

claims.feature: thematic core: the heart in conflict
claims.claim: Martin quotes Faulkner that the only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself, which drives his interior POV.
claims.source: Austin Chronicle, Amy Gentry interview (2013-08-29)
claims.quote: the human heart in conflict with itself

claims.claim: Martin cites the Iliad as a model where the hero of one side is the villain of the other, shaping his multi-sided viewpoint scheme.
claims.source: Adria's News interview (2012-10-08), repost
claims.quote: The hero of one side is the villain

claims.claim: After a decade of cutting scripts to 46 minutes Martin wanted breathing room, something big, rich and grand in scale, which explains the books' length and detail.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Outland (Ottakars) interview (Sept 2000)
claims.quote: something that was big and rich and grand in scale

claims.claim: Martin says ten years of cutting and trimming scripts to a tight fit preceded the deliberately expansive novels.
claims.source: Beatrice.com interview, Ron Hogan (2000)
claims.quote: cutting and trimming and making scripts into a very tight fit

claims.claim: Returning to prose, Martin says everything TV cannot afford becomes possible because the novelist is director and special effects at once.
claims.source: NYT ArtsBeat interview (2011-04-01)
claims.quote: You're the director, you're the special effects

claims.feature: gardener composition; discovery in the writing
claims.claim: Martin works without a detailed outline and locates the writing itself in determining events as much as choosing words.
claims.source: Beatrice.com interview, Ron Hogan (2000)
claims.quote: every word comes with a few drops of blood

claims.claim: Martin says the first chapter came out in about three days almost in the form readers have it.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: almost in the form you've read

claims.feature: hard scenes written out of order
claims.claim: Martin could not write the Red Wedding in sequence, wrote the rest of the book first, and calls it the hardest scene he ever wrote.
claims.source: CBS 60 Minutes, Anderson Cooper (2019-04-14)
claims.quote: That was the hardest scene I ever had to write.

claims.claim: Martin says he tries to make deaths unexpected and felt, in contrast to deaths that are mere statistics.
claims.source: CBS 60 Minutes, Anderson Cooper (2019-04-14)
claims.quote: I try to make you feel the deaths

claims.claim: Martin says he describes sex with the same explicit detail as an axe entering a skull and that only the sex draws complaints.
claims.source: The Mary Sue (2012-07-27), quoting via Boing Boing; original outlet untraced
claims.quote: I can describe an axe entering a human skull

claims.claim: Fire & Blood was easier because it is told in one voice, Archmaester Gyldayn's, unlike the novels' per-chapter voices.
claims.source: Entertainment Weekly (James Hibberd, 2018-11-19) via Winter Is Coming
claims.quote: I only have one voice to do.

claims.claim: Martin says ideas are cheap and execution is all-important; he borrows from the Wars of the Roses and hopes the blend becomes his own.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: it's the execution that is all-important

claims.claim: Martin treats SF and fantasy trappings as interchangeable furniture over the same storytelling craft.
claims.source: Locus Online interview excerpts (Nov 2005)
claims.quote: Sometimes the difference is just the furniture.

claims.claim: At NYCC 2025 Martin called Tolkien the most influential writer in his life and disputed the online feud narrative.
claims.source: Popverse, NYCC 2025 panel report (2025-11-05)
claims.quote: Tolkien is the most influential writer in my life.

claims.claim: Asked what matters most Martin answers characters but says he does not discount style and plot.
claims.source: SFFWorld interview, Dag R. (2006-05-17)
claims.quote: I don't discount the importance of style and plot

claims.claim: A critic finds Martin consistently chooses Anglo-Saxon-derived words and avoids Latinate vocabulary, producing a cumulative feel of antiquity.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style' (2014-03-31)
claims.quote: consistently chooses words of Anglo-Saxon origin

claims.claim: The same critic describes Martin's default style as lucid, functional, modern-thriller prose with occasional passages of powerfully simple beauty.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style' (2014-03-31)
claims.quote: lucid and functional

claims.claim: The critic faults unpredictable veering between fake medievalisms ('oft', 'elsewise', 'much and more') and modern colloquialisms like 'divvied up'.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style' (2014-03-31)
claims.quote: fake medievalisms

claims.claim: Confrontations are carried by terse, charged dialogue that produces sudden shocks of recognition.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style' (2014-03-31)
claims.quote: terse, charged dialogue

claims.claim: Martin relies on un-/be-/a- prefixes and -craft/-dom/-hood/-ship suffixes and coins Anglo-Saxon compounds (ironborn, sellsword, weirwood), reserving Latin/Greek forms for learned or religious contexts.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Affixes, compound and combination words' (2013-03-08)
claims.quote: systematic exclusion from his vocabulary

claims.claim: The density of invented compounds is what carries the reader into the secondary world, not stock medievalisms like 'prithee'.
claims.source: Books & Boots (Simon), 'Affixes, compound and combination words' (2013-03-08)
claims.quote: the greater the sense of moving into his otherworld

claims.claim: An essay reads Martin's recurring formulae ('black as night', 'faces still as masks', 'corded with muscle') as Homeric epithets that keep pace at the cost of memorable sentences.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer' (undated)
claims.quote: almost hypnotic readability

claims.claim: The same essay argues Martin prioritizes rhythm and momentum over sentence polish, so description is forgettable while dialogue excels.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer' (undated)
claims.quote: sentences aren't beautiful

claims.claim: A hostile reviewer lists 'jape' and 'mummer's farce' among words Martin rides like a hobbyhorse, and calls the prose at best serviceable.
claims.source: The Erstwhile Philistine, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin' (2012-03-21)
claims.quote: rides like a hobbyhorse

claims.claim: The same reviewer finds the sex scenes reliant on clichés such as 'drunk with desire'.
claims.source: The Erstwhile Philistine, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin' (2012-03-21)
claims.quote: drunk with desire

claims.claim: 'Words are wind' appears thirteen times in A Dance with Dragons across every region and faction, which the essay reads as deliberate motif.
claims.source: Overthinking It, 'Words are Wind: Repetition of Language in A Dance With Dragons' (2011-08-17)
claims.quote: no writer uses a phrase thirteen times by accident

claims.claim: Commenters on that essay counter that Martin has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language and, once he likes a term ('much and more', 'leal'), uses it everywhere.
claims.source: Overthinking It comments (2011-08)
claims.quote: GRRM has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language

claims.claim: The same thread credits Martin with strong leitmotifs, notably Reek's rhyme refrain.
claims.source: Overthinking It comments (2011-08)
claims.quote: he does do leitmotifs extremely well

claims.claim: A lexicographer notes 'ser', 'southron' and 'craven' are 15th-century forms and 'turncloak' is Martin's coinage from 'turncoat'.
claims.source: OUPblog, Adam Pulford, 'Words are wind' (2012-04-16)

claims.claim: Recurring sayings ('Dark wings, dark words', 'Words are wind', 'Seven hells') characterize cultures, and dialogue stays in English with culture-specific idiom rather than invented tongues.
claims.source: OUPblog, Adam Pulford, 'Words are wind' (2012-04-16)
claims.quote: Dark wings, dark words

claims.claim: Grossman characterizes Martin by sudden reversals and a plotter's tension, with narration shot from many angles by a dozen narrators.
claims.source: Time, Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien' (2005-11-13)
claims.quote: fond of sudden reversals

claims.claim: Grossman ties the multi-narrator scheme to the gritty, many-sided politics, which he calls all real.
claims.source: Time, Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien' (2005-11-13)
claims.quote: Martin shoots the action from many angles, with a dozen narrators

claims.feature: epic sweep with small human drama (praise)
claims.claim: Grossman praises Martin's ability to hold epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama in the same frame.
claims.source: Time, Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien' (2005-11-13)
claims.quote: epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama

claims.claim: Brown finds too much repetition, unexceptional prose, and characters who share idioms regardless of class or continent.
claims.source: The Atlantic, Rachael Brown (July 2011)
claims.quote: too much repetition, unexceptional prose

claims.claim: David Orr in the NYT argued the books' length is unnecessary and damages both prose and plot mechanics; Wasson in the CSM called the prose concise but pithy.
claims.source: Wikipedia, A Dance with Dragons, Reception (aggregator citing NYT 2011-08-14 and CSM 2011-07-12)
claims.quote: it hurts Martin's prose and his plot mechanics

claims.claim: Hartinger calls the prose tight, clear and evocative and the individual chapter structure about as good as structure gets, faulting only scope.

claims.quote: renders the Eastern cultures in particular with Herodotean gusto

claims.claim: The fornication is unsentimental but has a certain imaginative élan (the purple-bearded drunk lapping wine off a wench's breasts).

claims.quote: unsentimental fornication that is not without a certain imaginative élan

claims.claim: Brutal, irreversible consequences for characters' actions are part of the epic's distinctive tone and feel more 'literary' than any television series.

claims.quote: brutal, irreversible real-life consequences

claims.quote: I simply didn’t care about these strangers

claims.quote: an arresting echo of the Greek notion

claims.claim: The theological preoccupations do not raise the books to Lord of the Rings' level of parable; the appeal is thematic ambition plus richly satisfying details.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: richly satisfying details

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a 'gardener' who has a rough destination but improvises, in contrast to Tolkien the 'architect' who built languages and histories first.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: he has a rough idea where he’s going but improvises

claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I’ve invented seven words of High Valyrian

claims.claim: Martin drew on the Wars of the Roses rather than mythology, used relatively little magic, and the result felt dangerous, lusty and real.

claims.quote: it felt dangerous, lusty, and real

claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: Maybe I’m rewriting too much

claims.claim: Aligning the chronologies of seventeen viewpoint characters' travel times across two books bedevils the writing.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The ‘Dance’ timeline alone is a bitch and a half

claims.claim: Fans catch small continuity slips (a horse that changes sex, eyes green then blue) because every line is analysed.

claims.quote: People are analyzing every goddam line in these books

claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I like the pageantry and the color

claims.claim: More than a thousand named characters exist by a superfan's count; Martin quotes Tolkien that the tale grew in the telling.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The tale grew in the telling

claims.claim: The prose is shoddy and inconsistent while also being heavily repetitive.

claims.claim: Readers themselves mock recurring formulas such as 'as useless as nipples on a breastplate'.

claims.quote: as useless as nipples on a breastplate

claims.quote: behind the ostentatious fluff, there’s little substance

claims.claim: Martin is obsessed with expendable details (every feast dish, a character's gynecomastia), which bloats the books.

claims.quote: completely obsessed with expendable details

claims.quote: No literary devices such as symbolism, metaphors, even the fucking pacing

claims.claim: The duel's repeated 'You raped her. You murdered her. You killed her children' refrain is reproduced at length as evidence of flat, unbuilt violence.

claims.claim: The summary verdict is that the prose is not poetic, the dialogue can be childish and the story convoluted.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: His prose is not poetic, his dialogue can be childish

claims.claim: Because viewpoint characters must lack foresight of their fate, POV status itself predicts tribulation and makes the 'anyone can die' twists predictable.

claims.quote: readers already expect their POV characters to experience tribulation

claims.claim: Jaime's 'arc' is perception development: Martin warps the reader's view via backstory rather than changing the character.

claims.quote: What passes off as “character development” is actually “perception development.”

claims.claim: Characters are one-dimensional, focused on singular interests, and sortable into a 'Hall of Tropes' (Patriarch, Ideal Hero, Ax-Crazy).

claims.quote: one-dimensional and comically focused on singular interests

claims.claim: Dany reads as a white saviour whose errors cost her little, and Drogo as a Noble Savage; the essay is about characterization and politics, not sentence craft.

claims.quote: a feminist icon she ain’t

claims.claim: The books are great and hold a mirror to our world but suffer from the faults they try to expose.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011
claims.quote: These books are great

claims.quote: so hobbled by their brevity

claims.quote: could have been written as hearsay in other POV characters’ chapters

claims.quote: flagons ’n’ dragons, and swords ’n’ sorcerers

claims.quote: a comparative anthropology of sellsword companies. It’s exhausting

claims.quote: The constant punning on Reek

claims.quote: a cartoon psychopath, but a genuinely effective one

claims.quote: have to forget their names and learn new ones

claims.quote: names like “Pyat,” “Xaro Xhoan,” and “Jhogo,”

claims.quote: The default setting of Martin’s style is lucid and functional

claims.quote: a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness

claims.quote: ‘Among’ and ‘while’ become the archaic ‘amongst’ and ‘whilst’

claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term

claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style

claims.claim: Confrontations are done through terse, charged dialogue that delivers real dramatic shock.

claims.quote: terse, charged dialogue

claims.claim: Repeated 'cool' and 'still' in the Water Gardens passage may be haste or deliberate torpor-evoking repetition.

claims.quote: signs of haste, or careful repetitions

claims.claim: Names in three registers (near-familiar, alien, exotic) work on a purely verbal level to pull the reader into a parallel universe.

claims.claim: The style is uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative.

claims.quote: uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative

claims.claim: The archaic feel comes from the systematic exclusion of almost all Latin-, Greek- and French-derived words.

claims.quote: the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book

claims.claim: The prose is what holds Martin back from being a truly great author despite strong storytelling.

claims.quote: his prose holds him back from being a truly great author
